title: Microprofile: latency-to-throughput mapping playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is an operational playbook-style notebook for mapping latency percentiles to achievable throughput under realistic runtime conditions. The goal is to provide a small, reproducible toolkit (heuristics + config examples) we can use to answer: at what client concurrency / qps / batch size does p95 cross our SLO? Which resource or scheduling knob correlates most strongly with the knee in the curve?

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers carrying out throughput experiments
- Bench team validating new kernel/quantization changes
- Perf reviewers preparing PRs that alter scheduling or batching

High level approach (one-liner):
- Collect a tight, reproducible sweep of load points while capturing fine-grained resource telemetry and per-request latency histograms; correlate pxx inflection points with CPU/GPU util, kernel stalls, queue depth, and KV cache hit-rate.

Quick checklist (run before each sweep):
- [ ] Stabilize system clocks on all loadgen + runner nodes (ntpd/chrony).
- [ ] Disable dynamic frequency scaling on CPUs (set governors to performance) and pin CPU turbo settings to match prior runs.
- [ ] Ensure GPUs are in persistent mode (nvidia-smi -pm 1) and ECC mode as required by the test profile.
- [ ] Clear model cache and restart serving process between long sweeps.
- [ ] Record git SHA for serving runtime + kernel selection logs.
- [ ] Reserve a thermal-cooled machine for long runs to avoid fan-induced variance.

Load generation recipe (repeatable, low-noise):
- Tool: our internal loadgen (bench-driver) or gh/benchmark-harness. Prefer bench-driver v2.1+ for jitter mitigation.
- Seed policy: deterministic RNG seed (seed=42); for stochastic prompts use fixed prompt set files.
- Arrival pattern: use constant-qps with Poisson jitter option off for baseline. For realism run a separate wave with Poisson arrivals to measure tail sensitivity.
- Warmup: 3 phases
  1) Cold probe: 10 short requests at 1qps to bring filesystem and model artifacts into RAM.
  2) Priming ramp: linear ramp from 5% -> 50% target load over 120s. Purpose: build KV cache and transient JIT paths.
  3) Steady primer: hold 50% target for additional 180s with full telemetry capture.
- Steady samples: after warmup, run each point for at least 5 minutes to collect stable histograms; record at 1s resolution metrics. For long-run stability, run 30m points at key breakpoints.

Recommended sweep grid (example):
- Sweep metric: concurrency (clients) and qps. Map both: choose a target sequence such as [1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64] clients with a fixed request size; also sweep qps [5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160] for per-client variable pacing experiments.
- Batch size exploration: run each point with batch_size in [1, 2, 4, 8] and join curves.
- Model variants: native fp16, int8-quantized, and kernel-fused variant if present.

Telemetry to capture (minimum):
- Per-request latency histogram (p50/p90/p95/p99) from the serving process.
- GPU metrics (nvidia-smi + DCGM): util, mem_used, sm_efficiency, encoder/decoder activity, power draw.
- CPU metrics: per-core util, softirq, iowait, IRQ, C-state residency.
- IPC counters and context switches (perf stat sample).
- Kernel stalls: nvprof/NSight or tracepoints to detect long memcpy/host-to-device stalls when available.
- Serving internals: batch queue depth, batch coalescing delays, number of merges, KV cache hit/miss counters per request prefix.
- Network: NIC queues (tx/rx drops), kernel TX ring fullness, and GSO offload stats if applicable.

Correlation heuristics (what to look for):
- If p95 jumps while GPU util < 85%: likely queueing at software batching/lock contention or host-side stalls. Check batch queue depth and host threads.
- If p95/p99 climbs with GPU util saturating (~96–100%): throughput knee is GPU-bound; try increasing batching or using quantized kernels.
- If tail increases along with GPU memory spikes: KV cache thrashing or excessive activation memory growth. Use smaller sequence length or increase KV cache capacity.
- If p90 stable but p99 jumps irregularly: investigate async IO or background GC in the runtime. Look for periodic spikes in RSS or page faults.

Microprofile technique (how to pinpoint the bottleneck quickly):
1) Narrow the search: run the same qps with a stripped-down runtime (single-threaded host loop, no background metrics collection) — if latency improves, the host collector/observer is contributing noise.
2) Host vs device isolation: run a synthetic kernel stub that executes on GPU but without model work to measure baseline kernel dispatch overhead. Compare with real model to isolate kernel-time vs transfer-time.
3) Batch queue stress test: push a tight loop of small requests to saturate the queue and capture queue depth histogram; correlate depth with per-batch processing time.
4) Memory fence / memcpy test: measure host->device memcpy times under load using pci-e counters and nvprof; intermittent spikes point to PCIe contention or NUMA mis-affinity.

Practical knobs to iterate (ordered by low-to-high risk):
- Increase client-side pacing granularity (reduce burstiness).
- Tune batch_coalescer.max_wait_ms down to prioritize latency at the cost of some GPU throughput.
- Pin host worker threads to CPU cores - use core isolation for CVM-bound paths.
- Adjust quantization fallback thresholds to prefer int8 for non-critical requests.
- Enable memory prefetch / warmup for KV caches before ramping to peak.
- As a last resort, increase GPU allocation or move to a kernel variant tuned for high-occupancy.

Reproducibility notes and run metadata (capture with every run):
- bench-run-id: UUID
- bench-driver version
- serving binary SHA (git rev-parse --short HEAD)
- kernel selection summary (from runtime logs)
- node firmware version and driver (nvidia-smi --query)
- prompt-set filename and RNG seed
- thermal status at start and end (sensors output)

Example run log snippet (annotated):
-- run-id: 2025-02-01T14:12Z --
grid: clients=[4,8,12,16,24]; batch=[1,2,4]; model=int8
notes: warmup(120s ramp -> 180s steady primer)
4 clients / batch1 -> p95=45ms p99=72ms gpu=42% cpu_sys=12% queue_depth_median=1
8 clients / batch1 -> p95=48ms p99=85ms gpu=68% cpu_sys=22% queue_depth_median=1
12 clients / batch1 -> p95=92ms p99=210ms gpu=92% cpu_sys=26% queue_depth_median=2 
12 clients / batch2 -> p95=34ms p99=88ms gpu=95% cpu_sys=20% queue_depth_median=4 -> conclusion: batching recovers latency and keeps p99 reasonable, knee was GPU-bound.

Common failure modes (and how to triage quickly):
- Run-to-run variance >10%: check thermal throttling and driver mismatches; run short 5min stability run at low qps to confirm baseline.
- Spiky p99 at low average load: look for background maintenance tasks in runtime (GC, checkpointing), check systemd timers.
- High host CPU spin: prime candidate is inefficient serialization or logging path; rerun with logging disabled.

Data capture format recommendation:
- All telemetry exported as newline-delimited JSON files per component with timestamps in ISO8601 and bench-run-id present. Example fields: {"ts":..., "bench_run":..., "component":"gpu", "gpu_util":..}. Use our bench-collector to ingest and push to s3/<bench-run-id>/ for later analysis.

Visualization & analysis primer:
- Plot p50/p95/p99 across qps with shaded error bars (min/max across runs).
- Plot GPU util stacked with mean batch_time and queue_depth as secondary axis.
- Use CDF overlays of request latencies for candidate points near the knee.
- Annotate plots with kernel/version changes and warmup phases.

Open questions and experiments to run next:
- Quantify variance introduced by DCGM sampling vs nvidia-smi polling; does DCGM sampling at 1s add measurable overhead?
- Can we implement a non-blocking memcpy path for kv cache prefetch to reduce host-side stalls?
- Is there a predictable relationship between queue_depth_percentile and batch_merge_latency that we can use to autotune max_wait_ms?

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Wire bench-driver to automatically snapshot runtime logs on p99 spikes (GH:repo/benchmark-harness#142).
- Add a quick start script that generates the run metadata template used by analysis notebooks.
- Share preliminary charts with performance guild (present at next perf sync).

Appendix: sample bench-driver invocation
bench-driver --model my-model-int8 --prompts ./sets/small_prompts.json --seed 42 --clients 12 --qps 120 --batch-size 2 --warmup-ramp 120 --warmup-steady 180 --steady-duration 300 --collect-dcgm --collect-perf --run-id ${RUNID} --out s3://bench-results/${RUNID}/

End of playbook.

(Informal notes: this doc is intentionally pragmatic / notebook-like. For a formal runbook we will extract stable bullet points and add to the serving-runtime playbooks folder.)
